title: Sustainable Burst Economy and Tenant Credits — PRD Draft
content:
Purpose
This doc proposes a tenant credit and burst-economy system for Redwood Dedicated that balances predictable reserved capacity with flexible, cost-aware burst options and stronger isolation guarantees. Unlike simple burst quotas or hard preemption, this design defines an explicit economic layer (credits + escrow) plus policy surfaces for fairness and graceful degradation. The goal is to reduce surprise cost/latency for customers, enable predictable capacity commitments, and provide clear operational playbooks for both product and ops teams.

Problem statement
- Tenants want guaranteed baseline throughput but also need occasional higher capacity for spikes. Current designs (headroom, soft burst) are ad hoc: hard to explain billing, unclear fairness, and sometimes noisy neighbor outcomes.
- Engineering / SRE need deterministic behaviors for eviction and preemption to maintain SLOs by tier.
- Sales / finance need predictable unit economics for reserved vs burst usage.

Goals
- Provide an explicit, auditable credit ledger that tenants purchase (or are allocated) and spend when they burst beyond reserved pools.
- Make burst behavior transparent: how credits are priced, decayed, and converted to capacity.
- Protect latency-critical tenants using QoS lanes that consume higher-value credits and get isolation guarantees.
- Offer an operator-facing escrow and reclaim workflow to reconcile cross-tenant transfers and disputes.
- Provide telemetry and billing signals so customers can tune reservations vs credit budgets.

Non-goals
- This doc does not replace Dedicated reservations or pricing model; it augments them.
- Not addressing deep hardware-level scheduling (kernel/GPU scheduling) — this sits in orchestration layer.

Key concepts
- Credit unit (CR): atomic currency representing capacity-time normalized to model/instance type (e.g., 1 CR = 1k token-ms on A100-80GB equivalent).
- Escrow pool: a managed ledger that can hold credits for a tenant and optionally allow delegated transfers between tenant projects or sub-teams inside an enterprise account.
- Fidelity tier: mapping between credit classes and isolation/QoS (gold/silver/bronze), where gold credits buy lane isolation and preemption protection.
- Burn policy: deterministic mapping from observed workload characteristics (tokens, concurrency, model family) to CR consumption.
- Decay and top-up: rules for periodic replenishment, credit expiration, and grace windows.

High-level user flows
1) Purchase / allocate: Tenant buys credits in Console or via API and places them into escrow. Credits have a class (gold/silver/bronze) and optional project tags.
2) Serve-time consumption: When tenant requests exceed reserved allocation, runtime checks ledger: if credits available, it authorizes use and deducts CR based on burn policy. If gold credits used, requests routed to latency-fenced lanes with extra isolation.
3) Overflow handling: If escrow depleted, apply configured fallback: throttle/queue, soft-preempt, or failover to hosted API.
4) Reconciliation: Daily batch job aggregates CR usage and maps to billing line-items; operator tools can query escrow history for disputes.

Detailed mechanics
- Credit pricing: Per-region and per-hardware SKU conversion tables will be defined; we will provide a cost-approximation API so customers can simulate CR burn for expected workloads. Pricing should be monotonic with hardware capability and model family.
- Burn formula: CR = base_rate(model_family, seq_len) * tokens + concurrency_surcharge(concurrency_bucket) + routing_fee(if cross-pool). Tables will be versioned.
- Fidelity mapping: Gold credits: reserved lanes (per-host isolation fences), higher preemption priority, and slower decay. Silver: shared lanes with soft isolation (headroom helpers). Bronze: best-effort.
- Escrow controls: Admins can pin credits to specific projects or allow intra-organization transfers with configurable approval flows. Transfers create immutable audit records.

Isolation & preemption model
- Isolation fences: For gold-credit consumption, the scheduler allocates capacity from a pre-warmed subpool tagged for that tenant or lane. This reduces latency variance but costs more credits.
- Soft-preemption: Instead of immediate kill, jobs are throttled down (reduce concurrency or injection of short-queue delays) and retried at lower priority. Preemption decisions consider SLO criticality (from tenant profile) and remaining credit balance.
- Eviction safeguards: Eviction of reserved workloads only allowed after exhausting configured grace budget and operator-defined notifications. Eviction events recorded in escrow history.

Operational tooling and console surfaces
- Console: purchase credits, visual credit ledger, simulate burn for a traffic profile, set fallback policy, set delegation rules, and map projects to fidelity tiers.
- API: Credit purchase, transfer, usage query, simulate; endpoints: /v1/credits/{tenant}/simulate, /v1/credits/{tenant}/transfer. (API names are provisional.)
- Alerts: Billing thresholds (80%, 100% burn), unexpected burn rate spikes, cross-project transfer attempts.
- SRE runbooks: Investigate sudden burn spikes, reconcile escrow disputes, emergency credit top-up flow.

Telemetry & billing
- Telemetry should include: CR burned per-minute, burn broken down by model, tokens, concurrency, lane type (gold/silver/bronze), region.
- Billing: daily aggregation of CR consumption into line items; show estimated USD conversion in Console. Keep raw CRs in invoices for audit.

Security & compliance
- All transfers and spend must be auditable and signed. Escrow access controlled via RBAC.
- Credit history retained per org for at least 90 days in Console, configurable per contract.

Metrics & success criteria
- Adoption: X customers (pilot) onboarded in Q1 pilot.
- Predictability: >90% of tenants' monthly overage usage explainable by credit purchases (vs unknown/hidden bursts).
- Fairness: No more than 1 SLO violation per month attributable to noisy neighbors for customers using gold credits.
- Ops overhead: Average time to resolve escrow dispute < 24 hours for pilot group.

Rollout plan (phased)
Phase 0 — Prototype (2 months): implement ledger, simple burn formula, ephemeral gold lanes on dev cluster, basic UI mockups.
Phase 1 — Pilot (3 months): onboard 5 customers (mix of AI startups and platform teams), add transfer APIs, daily billing reconciliation, SRE runbooks.
Phase 2 — General availability (2 months): region pricing, full fidelity mapping, console polish, SLA language for gold-tier lanes.
Phase 3 — Extensions (ongoing): marketplace-style credit brokerage between tenants (opt-in), energy-aware pricing (lower CR cost during low-carbon-hours), and inter-org delegated credits.

Open questions & trade-offs
- Pricing granularity: per-token vs per-inference vs per-concurrency unit — which aligns best with customer billing expectations?
- Complexity vs clarity: How to present CR tables so customers can reason about cost without deep infra knowledge?
- Marketplace risks: Allowing inter-tenant brokerage may introduce fraud or accounting complexity that requires stronger controls.

Next steps
- Product: finalize burn formula and initial pricing table for dev cluster; build Console mockups.
- Eng (serving/runtime): instrument per-request hooks to query ledger and return cost estimate without blocking critical request paths.
- SRE/ops: draft runbooks for emergency top-ups and dispute resolution; prepare telemetry dashboards.

Appendix: example tenancy scenario
- Tenant A has a 100-CR monthly allocation (reserved). During a product launch they consume +250 CR via purchased credits in escrow, electing 60% gold credits to protect critical routes and 40% silver for background tasks. Over the month, the ledger shows gold burn correlated with reduced P99 latency spikes; billing and Console highlight the cost drivers allowing the tenant to decide on increasing permanent reservations for the high-traffic routes.
